planting.note: Set dormant tubers 4-5 inches deep in rich, moist, humus-laden woodland soil in mid-spring, choosing a sheltered site protected from late frost and wind.

directions: This selection is a notably larger-growing form of the Himalayan cobra lily, with a stouter false stem and an oversized purple-black-and-green striped hood drawn into an extra-long whip-like tail. Three glossy, white-veined leaflets unfurl beneath the flower each spring before the plant goes summer-dormant once the tuber has stored enough energy. Site it in a humid, sheltered woodland spot with part sun to light shade and keep soil consistently moist through the growing season. All parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals, so keep tubers and berries away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the soil surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil under deciduous shade.

directions: A Louisiana-origin selection of the mottled-leaf trillium native to the lower Mississippi River valley, this cultivar carries the species' marbled bronze-and-green foliage beneath upright maroon flowers in earliest spring. It is slow to multiply by rhizome offsets but persists for decades once established in undisturbed leaf-litter soil. Grow in light shade under hardwoods where the ground stays cool and evenly moist through spring, then goes drier as the plant retreats underground by midsummer. Avoid disturbing the rhizome once planted, since trilliums resent transplanting.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil beneath deciduous cover; a 2012 Plant Delights/JLBG selection crossing north-Georgia and north-Florida genetics, noted for clumping into dense colonies of over 100 stems.

directions: This narrowleaf trillium selection forms tight, densely clumping colonies of upright maroon flowers held just above whorls of slender, mottled leaflets, a clustering habit distinct from the more loosely spaced wild populations. It emerges early and goes dormant by midsummer, typical of the species' compact growth cycle. Grow in light shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, and leave undisturbed once planted to let the clump slowly thicken by rhizome division. Mulch with leaf litter each fall to mimic its native woodland floor habitat.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil beneath deciduous cover.

directions: Another narrowleaf trillium introduction from the same breeding line, this selection carries deep maroon upright flowers over strongly mottled, lance-shaped leaflets and a quick-to-establish rhizome. It shares the species' short above-ground season, flowering in early spring before retreating underground by summer. Grow in light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich woodland soil and avoid overhead watering that can rot the shallow rhizome. Pair with ferns and other spring ephemerals that fill in after it goes dormant.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil under deciduous shade; currently in active retail availability at a specialty trillium nursery.

directions: A diminutive sessile-flowered trillium species distinguished from its relatives by subtle differences in leaf mottling and flower proportions studied by trillium taxonomists. Dark, upright flowers sit directly atop a low whorl of mottled leaves in early spring, typical of the sessile trillium group. Grow in light shade in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil beneath hardwoods, and avoid disturbing the rhizome once established. Like other woodland trilliums it spreads slowly and rewards patience over many seasons.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland or prairie-edge soil beneath open canopy; a 2013 Plant Delights/JLBG introduction with silver-and-olive mottled foliage.

directions: This selection of the sessile prairie trillium grows taller than typical wild populations, holding its upturned maroon petals well above a whorl of mottled, sharply pointed leaves. The species is naturally wide-ranging across the eastern and midwestern woodlands, and this clone was chosen for its vigor and reliable size. Grow in light shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil, where it tolerates slightly drier conditions than many other trillium species once established. Leave the rhizome undisturbed to let the clump slowly bulk up over the years.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil beneath deciduous cover.

directions: A natural-hybrid-derived selection combining traits of its sessile-flowered trillium parents, this cultivar bears recurved, strongly mottled leaflets beneath dark upright flowers in early spring. The hybrid vigor shows in its sturdier stems and slightly larger flower size compared to either parent species. Grow in light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich soil and mulch with shredded leaves to replicate its native forest floor. Division is slow, so plant in small groups for the fullest early effect.
